---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com>
Date: Thu, Feb 26, 2015 at 2:09 PM
Subject: Re: question on mirtCAT
To: Pierre Michel <aliasj...@gmail.com>

I see that, but I really wonder what use it could be to understanding the bank as a whole. If you really insist on doing this, here's the steps:

- Each person essentially gets their own 'customized item bank'. Rather than building 1 full CAT with all items, build a mirt object using only the observed items for that particular person using the population IRT parameters
- Using the complete data response vector (extracted out manually, so no NA's should be present) pass this to local.pattern instead of the full response with a mixture of NAs and responses
- Adjust whatever properties you like for the CAT to see how things would have behaved
- Repeat for all individuals, building a customized CAT for each person

That should accomplish your goal, though admittedly it is a bit awkward (but then, the question is kind of awkward too, so I guess it fits). Cheers.

Phil

On Thu, Feb 26, 2015 at 1:59 PM, <aliasj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Among the different CAT simulations approches, There is one called post hoc simulation (or "real data" simulation). This is described on this link http://iacat.org/content/research-strategies-cat . It seems that the CAT procedures may be simulated using the available response data.
>
> Pierre MICHEL

>
> Le 26 févr. 2015 à 19:20, Phil Chalmers <rphilip....@gmail.com> a écrit :
>
> >
> >
> > On Thu, Feb 26, 2015 at 10:59 AM, Pierre Michel <aliasj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > >
> > > Le jeudi 26 février 2015 15:07:26 UTC+1, Phil Chalmers a écrit :
> > > > Hi Pierre,
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Thu, Feb 26, 2015 at 8:50 AM, Pierre Michel <aliasj...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > Hello Phil,
> > > > >
> > > > > I would like to do multidimensional CAT (MCAT) simulations. I have already fitted a MIRT model on my data (9-factor model with correlated factors), estimated individuals thetas (or IRT scores which will be considered as my "true scores" to compare with the MCAT scores). I want to use a "real data" simulation approach, i.e use the observed item responses rather than use simulated patterns. To use the mirtCAT function it requires complete responses patterns. So is it necessary to impute the missing responses ? Can I simply perform the MCAT using only the complete ones ? Or is there another way to do ?
> > > >
> > > > I'm not sure I understand what you mean here. Each person was given a test, but the test was smaller for each individual than the total number of items, and therefore NA's should be used for items that were not observed. Now, you wish to pass these observed responses into a CAT? That doesn't make sense to me. What if an item is selected during the CAT where no observed response was realized (i.e., it turns out they have high ability, so a difficult item is selected, for which they originally did not respond to). That sorta blows the whole point of CAT out of the water, unless I'm missing something....
> > >
> > >
> > > I understand... I cannot use imputed patterns because some individuals with initial missing responses could have a non-missing response (in the CAT) for an item he would not initially respond ? So it is better to use only the individuals with complete patterns to perform CAT simulations (?).
> >
> > For simulations, you shouldn't be using previous response patterns anyway. Simulation evaluations are about determining how hypothetical individuals should respond in the CAT, and seeing how well population characteristics can be recovered. For observed individuals, population characteristics are not known anyway, and therefore don't add much.
> >
> > >
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > I have another question: what is the best method to transform the IRT scores into score on a 0-100 scale score ? I was thinking about a inverse-logit transformation, but the results are quite strange when I check some isolated observations (e.g. an individual who responds the maximal category on all items doesn't have necessarily the maximal score). Is it an effect of the factor intercorrelations ?
> > > >
> > > > I'm not really sure I understand this either. You can scale the scores using the standard transformation formula score = mu + sd*z, but bounding them between 0 and 100 is a little trickier, which is why companies like ETS generally don't do that (they usually set things to have a mean of something like 500, SD = 100, which generally avoids flooring affects). Perhaps something like a truncated normal would do, but I would advise against it. Cheers.
> > > >
> > >
> > > What about using the following transformation : score = [(max(z) - min(z)) / (z - min(z))] * 100 ?
> > > Anyway, is it normal to observe big differences between IRT scores and mean raw scores ? That's why I suppose there is an effect of the factor correlations on the latent traits estimations...
> >
> > I would still advise against that, because it seems to be about reference scoring rather than an invertible transformation (and depends on how variable your population is, as well as what estimators were used). The theta's are already in a linear and unbounded metric, so that property should be preserved. And yes, total scores can be very different from IRT scores, because the latter is based on a 0 centered metric (hence, shifts with the difficulty of the test).
> >
> > Phil
> >
> > >
> > > > Phil
> > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > Thank you for your consideration,
> > > > >
> > > > > Pierre

Hello again everyone,

I am trying to run a CFA using the mirt package. I have 3 substantial factors FA, FB, and FC as well as several general factors F1, F2, etc.

I would like to let the substantial factors correlate among each other, but model the remaining factors as uncorrelated to the substantial factors, but correlated among each other.

For 3+1 factors, I used:
model=mirt.model('FA=1-3
             FB=4-6
             FC=7-9
             F1=1-9
             COV=FA*FB*FC
             CONSTRAIN = (1-9,a4)')

which works perfectly fine, resulting in the following summary():
Factor correlations:
   FA    FB    FC     F1
FA 1.000 0.643 0.522  0
FB 0.643 1.000 0.566  0
FC 0.522 0.566 1.000  0
F1 0.000 0.000 0.000  1

When I add further factors (F2, F3, ...) and specify that I would like them to "correlate freely", this fails to achieve the same result. The model
model=mirt.model('FA=1-3
             FB=4-6
             FC=7-9
             F1=1-9
             F2=1-9
             COV=FA*FB*FC, F1*F2
             CONSTRAIN = (1-9,a4),(1-9,a5)')

yields the following summary():
Factor correlations:

   FA    FB    FC     F1 F2
FA 1.000 0.669 0.553  0  0
FB 0.669 1.000 0.589  0  0
FC 0.553 0.589 1.000  0  0
F1 0.000 0.000 0.000  1  0
F2 0.000 0.000 0.000  0  1

Any ideas on why the COV formulation (comma-delimited) doesn't work and how to spell it correctly?

Many thanks,

Kristian

messages.body_plain:
The RE plot is a relative efficiency, so it's the ratio between the two test information tracelines (use plot(mod, type = 'info') to see both curves). So in this plot, there is much more information about the second group in the lower ability range (up to 1.4x as much is seems), and more info for the first group in the higher ability range. Be wary though, you should only interpret this plot if the groups have been anchored and equated, otherwise this could be capturing the wrong information. Cheers.

Phil

It's possible, but I highly don't recommend it. Basically, you're supplying a central density location that is very far from the integration grid, so every value in the grid essentially gets a very small likelihood (and therefore numerical issues arise, and the individual likelihood equations are not well computed). That's why the first model has a much higher log-likelihood than the first. Transforming scores this way is something I would advise against, so you'd be better to just apply a linear transformation on the typical scores after they are computed (e.g., X = theta * 10 + 50). Cheers.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
I've made some strides on this in the development version on Github, which you are welcome to check out. Using the new gpcm_mats input, you can specify a list of scoring coefficients for each dimension in each item, so that should accomplish your goal. E.g., setting up an extreme negative response style for trait 2 but with a gpcm scoring in trait 1 could be done like so:

```
library(mirt)
mats <- list()
mats[1:20] <- list(matrix(c(0:4, 1,0,0,0,0), 5))
a <- matrix(c(rep(1, 10), numeric(20), rep(1, 10)), 20)
d <- cbind(0, matrix(rnorm(4*20), 20))
dat <- simdata(a, d, 1000, 'gpcm', gpcm_mats = mats)

model <- mirt.model('F1 = 1-10
                    F2 = 11-20
                    COV = F1*F2')

#standard partial credit
gpcm <- mirt(dat, model, 'gpcm')
coef(gpcm, simplify=TRUE) #coefs way off

# customized scoring matrix
gpcm_custom <- mirt(dat, model, 'gpcm', gpcm_mats = mats)
coef(gpcm_custom, simplify=TRUE) #coefs recovered here

anova(gpcm, gpcm_custom) #information alone, gpcm_custom look better
M2(gpcm)
M2(gpcm_custom)
```

Let me know if you have any questions. Cheers.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
They are completely incorrect about the |.4| rule for exploratory models, because of the rotational indeterminacy issue. Unless they are referring to the raw slopes after rotation, but even then I have not idea where that rule of thumb came from (there is no reference of that anywhere to my knowledge, and I would completely advise against it's use anyway since it's wholly arbitrary).

You should check the standardised solution first, not the raw coefficients, and more specifically check the standardized commonality value (h2, which is essentially an effect size ranging from 0 to 1) and the rotated factor loadings. The h2 value is actually the standardized MVDISC coefficient, which they may have heard of before. So, perhaps you should let them know, politely, that they are incorrect in their recommendation on where to start. MIRT is often just nonlinear factor analysis, and in that setting one should be looking at standardized estimates for EFA, and IRT is no different in that respect. Cheers.

Phil

You may want to look into the bfactor() function if those subscales have residual covariation.

>
> I read your paper (mirt: A Multidimensional Item Response Theory Package for the R Environment), I saw your example 4.1 with the mirt ( ) function. It appears that the results of mirt ( ) are similar to the results of traditional factor analysis.

Indeed it is a full information item factor analysis, and when the IRT model used is the graded response model (2PL as a special case) then then MIRT and factor analysis with a polychoric matrix (with weights applied) are asymptotically equivalent. Other for IRT models this isn't true though.

>
> For the steps of developing the short scale, I wonder whether I can select items with the high item-total correlation from each sub-scale in the original  data set to form the short scale first. Then I split the original data set into two and conduct mirt ( ) in each split data set to examine the factor structure of the short scale between split data set.

You could, but I generally prefer looking at all items at once in exploratory models and weeding things out from there.

>
> Finally, I want to examine the goodness of fit of the short scale. When I type M2, I find additional indicators for RMSEA: RMSEA_5 and RMSEA95 , what are the differences among RMSEA RMSEA_5 and RMSEA95?

90% confidence interval for the RMSEA version with the M2 statistic. Cheers.

Phil

Dear Phil,

I have a question concerning the simulation of data according the graded response model and the estimation of the M2 statistic for testing the model fit.

I performed 10 000 repetitions (looping with for)  of the following calculation:

#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Simulate data according to the graded response model

library(mirt)

ol <- matrix(rlnorm(15, .2, .3))

ci <- matrix(rnorm(15*3, 0, 2), 15)

ci <- t(apply(ci, 1, sort, decreasing=TRUE))

poly.grm <- simdata(ol, ci, 200, itemtype = 'graded')

# 2. dichotomization of the data [1 & 2 = 0] & [3 & 4 = 1]

dich.grm <- ifelse(poly.grm < 3,0,1)

# 3. estimation of the graded response model for the polytomous and dichotomized data

est.grm.poly <- mirt(poly.grm, model=1, itemtype="graded")

est.grm.dich <- mirt(dich.grm, model=1, itemtype="graded")

# 4. calculation of the M2 statistic for testing the model fit

# p-values which are smaller than alpha are coded as 1, else 0

alpha <- 0.05

m.grm.poly <- M2(est.grm.poly)

p.grm.poly <- m.grm.poly[,3]

alpha.grm.poly <- ifelse(p.grm.poly < alpha,1,0)

m.grm.dich <- M2(est.grm.dich)

p.grm.dich <- m.grm.dich[,3]

alpha.grm.dich <- ifelse(p.grm.dich < alpha,1,0)

#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The results were surprisingly. The M2 statistic (for testing the model fit) had significant p-values in 2129 from 10000 (0.2129) cases when calculating the polytomous model,

but only 570 from 10000 (0.057) significant p-values when calculating the dichotomous model.

How can that be? Have I made a mistake in the calculation?

Thank you very much for your Help.

Best regards Isabell

Error in FUN(newX[, i], ...) :
  Items contain category scoring spaces greater than 1.

This is because with N=200, and the way the intercepts were defined in the GRM (see here for a better method: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/mirt-package/simdata/mirt-package/nCvEbML0OaA/jjNw-qtQx8EJ), each item likely dropped responses or kept so few to cause estimation issues. Models that fail to converge should not be tested for goodness of fit.

Phil
